n: Hezekiah invited all Israel and Judah — even the northern tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh — to Jerusalem to keep the Passover. He reached across the old division to reunite God’s people in worship.

f.g: Leading northern tribes, representing the remnant of the northern kingdom after Assyria’s conquest.

n: The king, officials, and assembly decided to hold Passover in the second month instead of the first.

f.g: The law allowed a second-month Passover for those unable to keep it on time.

n: They couldn’t hold it at the normal time because not enough priests had been purified and the people hadn’t yet gathered.

f.w: the priests had not sanctified themselves sufficiently

n: The plan pleased the king and the whole assembly.
They proclaimed it from Beersheba to Dan — the whole land — because Passover hadn’t been kept as prescribed for a long time.

f.g: From the far south to the far north — all Israel.

n: Couriers carried letters urging: Israel, return to the Lord, and He will return to you — the remnant who escaped Assyria. Turning to God brings God turning to us.
Don’t be like your fathers and brothers who were unfaithful and were given over to ruin, as you can see for yourselves.
Don’t be stubborn like your ancestors; yield to the Lord, come to His sanctuary, and serve Him, so His anger turns away.

f.g: Stubborn, like an ox refusing the yoke.
Literally ‘give the hand to the LORD’ — pledge yourselves.

n: If you return, your exiled relatives will find mercy from their captors and come home, for the Lord is gracious and merciful and will not turn His face away. A promise of gathering for those who return.

f.w: the LORD your God is gracious and merciful

n: The couriers went town to town through Ephraim, Manasseh, and Zebulun, but most people laughed at and mocked them.
Still, some from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem. Humility opens the way back.
In Judah, God’s hand gave the people unity of heart to obey the king and officials, who followed the Lord’s word.
A huge crowd gathered in Jerusalem for the Feast of Unleavened Bread in the second month.
First they removed the pagan altars and incense altars Ahaz had set up all over Jerusalem and threw them into the Kidron Valley.

f.w: the altars that were in Jerusalem

n: They slaughtered the Passover lambs on the fourteenth of the second month. Priests and Levites, ashamed of their lack of readiness, purified themselves and brought burnt offerings. The people’s zeal shamed the clergy into action.
Priests and Levites took their places according to Moses’ law; the priests sprinkled the blood that the Levites handed to them.
Many in the crowd were not ritually clean, so the Levites slaughtered the Passover lambs for them to keep the offering holy.
Many northerners ate the Passover without proper purification — contrary to the law. But Hezekiah prayed: “May the good LORD pardon everyone…”

f.w: The good LORD pardon every one

n: “…who sets his heart to seek God, even if not purified by the sanctuary’s rules.” Hezekiah understood God values a sincere heart above ritual technicalities.

f.w: That prepareth his heart to seek God

n: The Lord heard Hezekiah and healed the people. God honored a prayer of mercy for sincere seekers.
Israel kept the seven-day feast with great joy, and the priests and Levites praised the Lord daily with loud instruments.
Hezekiah encouraged the Levites who taught the good knowledge of the Lord. All week the people ate, offered peace offerings, and gave thanks (or confessed) to God.

f.g: Spoke encouragingly; literally ‘spoke to the heart.’
Giving thanks or confessing — the Hebrew can mean both.

n: The whole assembly decided to celebrate seven more days, and did so joyfully. Joy in worship was so great they didn’t want it to end.
Hezekiah gave 1,000 bulls and 7,000 sheep, and the officials gave 1,000 bulls and 10,000 sheep. Many more priests purified themselves.

f.g: Contributed as offerings for the people’s feasting.

n: Everyone rejoiced — Judah, priests and Levites, those from Israel, and foreigners living among them. A celebration of unity.

f.g: Resident foreigners who had joined Israel’s worship.

n: Jerusalem hadn’t seen such joy since the days of Solomon — the temple’s dedication.
The priests and Levites blessed the people, and their prayer reached God’s holy dwelling in heaven. The temple on earth was linked to God’s home above.

f.w: his holy dwelling place, even unto heaven
